What is Extensions

Extensions is the developer-facing extensibility model that allows engineers to build, deploy, and register custom Behaviors and Controllers within the pipeline. Extensions follow the same contracts, decorators, and lifecycle hooks used by built-in add-ons, ensuring that custom code participates in pipeline execution with full orchestrator and Conductor support.

Extensions are not a separate runtime or plugin system. They are first-class pipeline participants that implement BehaviorContract<T> or ControllerContract<T>, are decorated with @VaultBehavior or @VaultController, and are registered in the FeatureCell declaration alongside built-in add-ons. The orchestrator and Conductor discover, validate, and execute Extensions exactly as they do core and add-on pipeline units.

This model allows teams to address domain-specific requirements—such as custom merge strategies, specialized error handling, rate-limiting policies, or gated approval workflows—without modifying internals.

Why Extensions

The built-in add-on library covers common concerns such as caching, distinct-until-changed operators, deep merge strategies, throttling, and delay-based rate limiting. However, production applications frequently encounter requirements that are unique to a specific domain, organization, or integration surface.

Extensions exist so that engineers can implement those requirements using the same pipeline guarantees that built-in add-ons rely on:

  • Stage isolation — Custom Behaviors execute only within their declared pipeline stage and cannot interfere with other stages.
  • Deterministic ordering — The orchestrator enforces execution order based on stage classification, not registration order.
  • Lifecycle management — Construction, reset, and destroy hooks are called automatically by the orchestrator and Conductor.
  • Fluent configuration — Extensions integrate with the FeatureCell fluent API for type-safe, chainable configuration.
  • Tooling and diagnostics — Extensions are visible to DevTools, diagnostics, and introspection APIs through their declared keys.
What Can Be Extended

The pipeline supports two categories of extensions:

Custom Behaviors

Behaviors are stage-bound units of responsibility that perform work within a specific pipeline stage. A custom Behavior can target any supported stage, including:

Behavior Type Description
Extension General-purpose Behaviors that add methods to the FeatureCell API surface.
Interceptor Behaviors that observe or react to pipeline events such as errors.
Merge Behaviors that define custom merge strategies for combining current and incoming state.
Operator Behaviors that apply RxJS operators to the emission stream.
Encrypt Behaviors that apply encryption or decryption transformations to state values during pipeline processing.
ErrorTransform Behaviors that transform or enrich error objects before they are dispatched to error callbacks.
Persist Behaviors that persist committed state to external storage such as localStorage, sessionStorage, or IndexedDB.
ReplayGlobalError Behaviors that replay previously captured global errors into the pipeline for reprocessing or observation.
StepwiseFilter Behaviors that conditionally suppress pipeline values using the stepwise bus coordination protocol.
StepwiseReducer Behaviors that derive or transform candidate values using the stepwise bus coordination protocol.
StepwiseResolve Behaviors that normalize incoming state inputs using the stepwise bus coordination protocol.

Custom Behaviors implement BehaviorContract<T> and are decorated with @VaultBehavior. For a complete list of extensible and restricted Behavior types, see Building Custom Behaviors.

Custom Controllers

Controllers are coordination authorities that mediate pipeline execution through a voting model. A custom Controller can implement policies such as:

Controller Type Description
Error Controllers that define error-handling policies for the pipeline. Only one Error Controller may be active per FeatureCell.
Policy Controllers that enforce pipeline execution policies such as rate limiting, circuit breakers, concurrency gates, or approval workflows.
ReplayGlobalError Controllers that coordinate the replay of previously captured global errors back into the pipeline.
Stepwise Controllers that coordinate stepwise bus interactions, mediating multi-phase pipeline resolution through the voting model.

Custom Controllers implement ControllerContract<T> and are decorated with @VaultController. For a complete list of extensible and restricted Controller types, see Building Custom Controllers.

Extension Anatomy

Every Extension—whether a Behavior or Controller—follows a consistent structural pattern:

  • A decorator (@VaultBehavior or @VaultController) that declares metadata such as type, key, criticality, and configuration requirements.
  • A contract implementation (BehaviorContract<T> or ControllerContract<T>) that defines the Extension's runtime behavior.
  • An options interface that describes the configuration the Extension accepts through the fluent API.
  • A fluent API installer (installFluentApi) that registers a chainable configuration method on the FeatureCell.
  • An optional module augmentation that extends TypeScript's type surface so consumers receive full IntelliSense for new FeatureCell methods and fluent configuration.

This pattern is identical for built-in add-ons and custom Extensions. There is no separate plugin API, registration ceremony, or runtime discovery mechanism.

Build from Scratch vs Extend Existing

Engineers have two approaches when creating custom pipeline participants:

Implement the Contract Directly

The recommended default. Implement BehaviorContract<T> or ControllerContract<T> directly and apply the appropriate decorator. This gives full control over the Extension's logic and lifecycle.

Extend an Existing Class

When an existing built-in Behavior or Controller already provides most of the required logic, extend its concrete class and apply a new decorator with a unique key and configKey. The new decorator replaces the parent's metadata entirely, so the orchestrator or Conductor treats the subclass as a distinct pipeline participant.

This approach is useful for adding logging, adjusting thresholds, introducing conditional bypasses, or customizing a single method without reimplementing the entire Extension.

Note

Abstract base classes are available for Behavior families that share substantial internal mechanics. For example, StepwiseBehaviorAbstract<T> provides the shared stepwise bus coordination protocol used by withStepwiseResolveBehavior, withStepwiseFilterBehavior, and withStepwiseReducerBehavior. For most custom Extensions, implementing the contract interface directly is sufficient.

Registration

Extensions are registered by passing the class to the appropriate array in the FeatureCell declaration:

  • Custom Behaviors are added to the Behavior array (third argument).
  • Custom Controllers are added to the Controller array (fourth argument). 
{{`export const myCell = FeatureCell(
  MyCellToken,
  {
    key: 'my-cell',
    initialState: {}
  },
  [
    withMyCustomBehavior     // custom behavior
  ],
  [
    withMyCustomController   // custom controller
  ]
);

myCell
  .withMyCustomBehavior({ /* options */ })
  .withMyCustomController({ /* options */ })
  .initialize();`}}

Extensions that are not registered in the FeatureCell declaration are not discovered, validated, or executed. There is no global registry or implicit activation.

Restricted Types

Not all Behavior and Controller types are available for custom Extensions. The Orchestrator and Conductor enforce strict boundaries between core pipeline infrastructure and the extensible surface. Behaviors or Controllers that belong to core pipeline stages are managed exclusively by the runtime and are silently removed if provided in the FeatureCell declaration.

For the complete list of restricted types, see Building Custom Behaviors and Building Custom Controllers.
